causalChain: Import concentration or trade disruption constrains rare-earth feedstock and magnet availability; extraction projects can diversify ore supply only after resource conversion, permitting, financing, construction, recovery and transport. Capacity shortfalls can create input scarcity, higher costs, delayed production and weak returns that in turn threaten project financing.

causalChain: Permanent magnets embedded in vehicles, turbines, appliances and equipment enter the in-use stock for years; product lifetime, collection, disassembly and sorting determine when and how much magnet scrap becomes feed. Recovery and separation yields determine secondary rare-earth output; demand can grow faster than this lagged waste flow, so new recycling plants may initially compete for limited feedstock. Recycling can reduce virgin imports over time but cannot be inferred from generic waste recycling rates or nameplate capacity.
counterEvidence: The Commission identifies <1% EU rare-earth recycling and also reports that Carester, Solvay and Inspiree could contribute about 3,800 tonnes of rare-earth permanent magnets, around 20% of then-current demand, in coming years if feedstock and incentives are in place. This supports potential material contribution; it is a conditional projection, not a realized end-of-life input rate. Manufacturing scrap and imported secondary material may provide additional feed beyond retired EU products if correctly traced. Solvay’s 2025 primary press release does state a corporate objective of meeting 30% of European rare-earth demand by 2030 and reports the La Rochelle line’s commercial start; it does not attribute that objective to recycling alone, give a demand denominator or report achieved output. This likely creates/echoes ambiguity with the alleged ~30% recycling-sufficiency claim; it cannot replace the missing mass balance. The available CEPS cohort model provides source-linked scenario bounds: selected-application secondary supply equals 8-19% of demand in 2025-2030, 16-34% in 2040 and 24-48% in 2050. These challenge a precise 30% claim but remain scenario outputs, not observed throughput or probabilities; the 2030 theoretical EOL availability is about 10 kt against 36 kt modeled selected-application demand.
stockFlowTransmission: The end-of-life stream is a delayed function of historic sales/installation cohorts, product magnet intensity, trade, lifespan and collection share. Available feed is not the same as recoverable material; multiply by sorting/disassembly capture, magnet recovery, separation/refining yield and quality acceptance. Secondary material flow then displaces a share of primary feed, subject to demand growth, export/import flows and stock accumulation. CRMA's 25% capacity benchmark has a different numerator and denominator from recycled input actually consumed. Cohort turnover delays feed: the CEPS model uses 13-year EV, 12-year conventional vehicle, 25-year onshore wind and 30-year offshore wind lives, with collection/dismantling scenarios by application. For EVs, the table uses 50/90% collection and 85/95% dismantling scenario rates; reported first large EV retirements begin around 2035, with roughly 10 kt/y of EV EOL magnet material by 2040. Manufacturing scrap is not in this EOL flow model. Do not equate magnet mass, contained element, oxide, metal or separated magnet output.
identificationLimits: EU-wide permanent-magnet dynamic material-flow series is not established by the accepted map. JRC methodology warns generic EOL recycling input and EOL recycling efficiency differ; JRC wind turbine projections cover one product stock and the UK study is not an EU estimate. Commission capacity projections rely on feedstock/incentive conditions. Recovery rates, trade in scrap and product-specific magnet content remain data gaps. CEPS model covers selected applications (about 68% of the overall magnet market in its 2020 estimate) and uses projected EV sales, assumed lifetimes and collection/disassembly, so its denominator and supply shares are incomplete scenarios. It does not establish actual current utilization, universal refining/recycling yield, plant feed economics, manufacturing-scrap flow, or complete Pr/Tb demand. JRC 2026 wind outflow is an element outflow estimate with lifetime sensitivity, not recycled production.
modelability: Use cohort-based material-flow accounting by application, with annual additions, import/export, magnet intensity, service life distributions, collection, disassembly and process yields. Reconcile physical inputs and outputs by material and stage, cap secondary production by available scrap, and scenario-test faster collection or substitution without assuming immediate end-of-life feed. Bounded scenario mass accounting is possible for selected cohorts using the CEPS demand/TRP and chain-level secondary-supply shares; keep its coverage and assumptions visible. Plant throughput, scrap and element-specific separated-oxide/metal yields should remain unknown parameters or explicit scenario assumptions rather than calibrated observations.
scenarioRelevance: Tests EU resilience claims and supply-chain adaptation over 2026–30. Short-run recycling is constrained by in-use stocks; medium/longer-run contribution can grow as installed EV and wind cohorts retire. This changes the time profile of import dependence, not simply the long-run target value. The evidence supplies plausible low/high supply-share envelopes (8-19% 2025-30, 16-34% 2040, 24-48% 2050) and a cohort lag useful for stress scenarios; it cannot justify a deterministic 30% recycling supply baseline.
unresolvedUncertainty: Need EU magnet demand by element/use, existing stock cohorts, product lifetime curves, collection and exports, manufacturing-scrap share, current plant feed contracts and process yields. The alleged ~30% sufficiency claim is not evidenced by this source set and cannot be confirmed or rejected quantitatively without matched demand and feedstock accounting. No public matched tonne denominator, supply split, output or recycling share is supplied. EU product-cohort stock, retirements, collection/export, scrap, yields and demand remain unassembled. causalChain: A global risk shock or relative-yield change alters bilateral CHF demand; the exchange rate then changes foreign-currency revenue and input costs, importer prices, exporter markups and volumes, and monetary conditions. SNB FX intervention and policy rates can alter or lean against the move. The direction depends on the countercurrency and shock, not a single global CHF index.
counterEvidence: SNB safe-haven estimates find appreciation against EUR and carry currencies but depreciation against USD, JPY and GBP in stress; relationships vary over time. SNB reported a recent CHF depreciation supportive of exchange-sensitive exporters. The 2022 current-account paper finds headline current account largely inelastic at business-cycle frequency despite negative effects on exposed-sector profits and consumer prices. Latest SNB monthly averages for Sep 2026 (released 1 Oct) were CHF 0.94312/EUR and CHF 0.81926/USD; these levels alone do not establish appreciation over a chosen base, and the 2015 study finds bilateral rather than universal safe-haven behavior. In the 2015 synthetic-control study aggregate real export quantities were not significantly reduced despite about -7% short-run nominal CHF exports; pharma/chemicals and engineering/instruments differed.
stockFlowTransmission: Existing foreign-currency assets, liabilities, export receivables and imported-input payables revalue immediately; hedges, currency denomination and balance-sheet currency matching change the net cash effect. Price/volume and market-share flows respond over contracts, inventory and customer substitution horizons. A current-account balance is a flow, not a direct estimate of wealth or domestic output.
identificationLimits: Historical safe-haven regressions are currency-pair and sample dependent; common risk shocks confound bilateral exchange-rate moves. The 2015 policy discontinuity is unusually sharp and cannot identify every future shock. The current-account elasticity paper isolates exchange-rate variation but estimates aggregates that mask exposed sector profits, prices, gold trade and income offsets. A current bilateral monthly-average level is available, not a causal estimate; the 2015 floor-removal event is an unusually clean but one-off treatment. The 2025 synthetic-control study reports approximately 10% EUR appreciation, +8% nominal EUR exports over 18 months, around -7% nominal CHF exports short-run and insignificant aggregate real quantity response; counterfactual assumptions, short sample and lack of comparable sector quantity deflators constrain transfer.
modelability: Medium: scenario logic can use bilateral EUR/CHF and USD/CHF shocks, with separate unhedged exposures, import content and lagged price/volume channels. Calibrating future shock probabilities or a single economy-wide CHF elasticity is not warranted from these sources.
scenarioRelevance: High for a Swiss safe-haven branch: a sharp EUR appreciation of CHF can lower import inflation while compressing exporters' margins and output. Compare with SNB intervention, recent depreciation and non-EUR countercurrency paths.
unresolvedUncertainty: No verified current firm-level currency invoice, hedge maturity, pass-through, imported-input, foreign asset/liability or sector exposure matrix was assembled in this extraction. The sign and magnitude of a 2026–30 risk episode depend on risk source, yields, SNB actions and the bilateral currency involved.
investigationNotes: Investigated safe-haven direction, policy endogeneity, imported-input offsets, current-account aggregation and export-profit evidence. SNB Working Paper 2013-04 explicitly limits the safe-haven claim to some bilateral rates; SNB WP 2022-14 finds current-account inelasticity but confirms consumer prices and exposed-sector corporate profits decline after appreciation. Retain this mechanism but do not translate ‘anchor’ into universal appreciation or assume a current-account collapse. Collect 2026 bilateral effective rates, intervention/reserve data, exporter currency shares and sector hedges for later calibration. Targeted repair extracted SNB devkum September 2026 monthly averages directly from the official CSV endpoint (EUR1=0.94312 CHF; USD1=0.81926 CHF, publication timestamp 1 Oct 2026). These are monthly averages, not spot closing rates. Brunhart and Geiger (2025), synthetic control of customs exports Jan 2015–Jul 2017, estimate for roughly 10% EUR/CHF appreciation: nominal EUR exports +about 8% by 18 months, nominal CHF exports about -7% short term, and aggregate real quantities statistically indistinguishable from the counterfactual. Pharma/chemicals showed flexible prices and no significant real quantity loss; engineering and precision instruments suffered more. Data/code are on request and sectoral real deflators are unavailable, so no current elasticity is applied.
dispositionRationale: FOCBS q/q period corrected; August detailed import indexes and computed changes verified. SNB net total current account, gross merchanting turnover and qualitative net-merchanting direction remain separate. Merchanting-only figure not located after documented endpoint searches; full search exhaustion is not claimed. Private finance/hedge data remain unknown. September import-price release falls after cutoff.

causalChain: CHF appreciation reduces the CHF price of foreign goods according to invoice currency and price-setting behavior; retailers and importers pass some change into consumer goods with lags. Energy, domestic services, rents, margins and the SNB policy response jointly determine CPI. CHF weakness or global commodity inflation can reverse the import disinflation contribution.
counterEvidence: 2015 transaction-level results show immediate complete pass-through for euro-invoiced imports and partial, rapid pass-through for CHF-invoiced goods, not full aggregate CPI pass-through. The 2007 VAR evidence finds import-price pass-through exceeds CPI pass-through and CPI sensitivity weakened in low/stable inflation. In September 2026 CPI inflation was 1.0% y/y, with SNB attributing the recent rise mainly to oil-product prices; the SNB forecast was revised higher partly due to energy and franc weakening. The September 2026 CHF exchange-rate level is not itself an import-price observation. SNB 2018 micro evidence around the >11% Jan 2015 shock found immediate, complete pass-through into euro-invoiced import unit values but only partial, exceptionally fast pass-through for CHF-invoiced goods (starting second working day and reaching medium-run pass-through after an average of 12 working days). Aggregate CPI pass-through is weaker in older VAR evidence; energy and administered prices can dominate monthly CPI. The latest FSO detailed import-price data available by 2026-10-14 cover August, while September CPI was 1.0% y/y. CPI release says heating oil, petrol and diesel rose, but this does not quantify an imported-goods CPI component or isolate CHF pass-through.

causalChain: Geopolitical fragmentation or supply restrictions can lead Swiss firms to diversify suppliers, inventories, production locations and customer markets toward trusted partners. Diversification can improve resilience but may increase costs, reduce scale economies or simply relocate concentration; openness and EU market access shape feasible options.
counterEvidence: OECD review highlights resilience and diversification tradeoffs; Switzerland's strong export performance and open international networks indicate that global integration remains a source of specialization and demand, not just vulnerability. No verified Swiss causal estimate shows friendshoring net benefits, and recent CHF/export and pharma output swings show non-supply channels can dominate. OECD’s measured structural evidence offers concrete counterweight to a generic vulnerability story: average Swiss import HHI fell 7% from 2002 to 2021; high-concentration imports accounted for a lower share than in early 2000s; Swiss foreign-input reliance is below OECD average across most sectors. At the same time, EU suppliers provided 54% and Asian suppliers 17% of imported intermediate inputs on average (2018 data), and about 60 product-country combinations remained flagged in 2021. Relocation claims must distinguish diversified sourcing and EU dependence from actual nearshoring. The OECD September 2026 Switzerland Survey says Switzerland weathered recent shocks comparatively well, while remaining vulnerable to international trade/geopolitical uncertainty. This current qualitative assessment supports resilience and exposure together, but is not a causal estimate of friendshoring.
stockFlowTransmission: Supplier/customer concentration, inventories, production capacity, specialized labor and FDI are stocks; orders, imports, exports, inventory replenishment, investment and earnings are flows. Diversification requires upfront capital and may lower short-run productivity while reducing tail loss from disruption. Financial-account FDI and portfolio transactions cannot be treated as physical supply relocation without company-level evidence. OECD import HHI/product-country flags and TiVA foreign-input shares map supplier concentration and upstream stocks; changes in sourcing, inventory, output, and investment are flows. OECD documents some Swiss firms sourcing critical Chinese inputs shifting purchases toward Europe or own European production, but this dated evidence is not a whole-economy friendshoring flow measure.

OECD 2024 reports data mainly through 2018–2021: imported intermediates averaged 54% EU, 17% Asia, 10% North America, 8% rest of Europe and 11% other; average import HHI fell 7% from 2002 to 2021 and about 60 high-risk country-product pairs remained flagged in 2021. The data indicate concentration/diversification, not changes caused by friendshoring. A planned nearshoring survey found in trade press/industry sources is not used as national evidence.
modelability: Low to medium until firm-level supplier origin/concentration, inventory, input-output exposure, logistics and substitution times are assembled. A scenario can bound disruption/reallocation costs and resilience benefits, but should label them assumptions and avoid a single net friendshoring coefficient.
scenarioRelevance: Medium: trusted-partner access may support Switzerland as a relative anchor, while concentrated pharmaceutical/chemical exports, EU market-access uncertainty, commodity trading and energy dependence expose it to geopolitical shocks.
unresolvedUncertainty: Current 2022–26 product-level import concentration, input origin at firm level, critical-input inventories, substitution lags, FDI plant relocation and whether the EU share reflects resilience or concentration remain unknown. causalChain: A policy/inflation/supply shock raises risk-free rates, term premia, FX basis or borrower-specific spreads; asset repricing and margin/collateral calls may constrain intermediaries; maturing liabilities then refinance at higher costs or fail to roll; weaker cash flow and investment can lower collateral and repayment capacity, creating lender losses and tighter credit. Central-bank facilities can bridge solvent institutions facing liquidity pressure, while fiscal restructuring, recapitalization or loss allocation is needed for insolvency.
counterEvidence: BIS measured cross-border bank credit was +11% y/y to USD 39.5tn at end-Q1 2026 and USD/EUR foreign-currency nonbank credit measures also grew. That rebuts contraction in those aggregates, not stress in marginal borrowers. High cash, fixed coupons, hedging, longer maturities, deposits, local markets and official backstops can dampen pass-through; the IMF April 2026 report described risks and amplification channels while noting markets had remained orderly to date.
stockFlowTransmission: Debt, liquid assets, collateral and capital are balance-sheet stocks; interest expense, new issuance, repayments, asset sales and credit growth are flows. For each borrower, track opening debt plus issuance minus principal repayment and write-offs, with FX/price valuation separated. Refinancing cost applies to new borrowing and maturing/reset debt, not instantly to every outstanding fixed-rate liability. Treat market depth/spreads separately from credit quantities.
identificationLimits: BIS GLI covers specified foreign-currency credit to nonbanks and BIS LBS locational banking positions; neither measures all global liquidity, domestic lending, shadow credit, market depth, borrower solvency or maturity. IMF GFSR risk mapping and financial-accelerator literature support channels but do not identify a 2026–30 aggregate causal multiplier. Common shocks, endogenous risk premia and policy response complicate identification.
modelability: Modelable as a segmented balance-sheet bridge with rate curves, borrower spreads, currency, maturity/reset schedules, hedges, cash, collateral haircuts and policy liquidity; aggregate credit growth is a descriptive check, not a calibration of defaults or output multipliers.
scenarioRelevance: Stress test sustained rates and spreads against actual refinancing needs and cash-flow buffers across regions; distinguish orderly repricing from funding-market discontinuity and solvency losses.
unresolvedUncertainty: Matched current debt-service, maturity, currency and nonbank leverage data are incomplete across US, China, EU and Switzerland. Q1 2026 BIS is the latest observation in the accepted cutoff bundle; Q2 is unavailable at cutoff. There is no defensible single observed global liquidity quantity or crisis threshold.
investigationNotes: Primary support combines the BIS July 31 2026 statistical release, IMF April 2026 GFSR risk-channel findings, the BIS reconstruction of pre-2008 non-US bank dollar funding gaps and Federal Reserve swap-line retrospective, plus financial accelerator theory. Counterevidence is explicit: BIS quantity growth and orderly market assessment do not show a current generalized collapse. Modeling should transmit policy/risk shocks only through documented maturity, currency, collateral and cash-flow exposure segments; keep liquidity assistance distinct from solvency. Do not convert correlation, a broad credit stock or a scenario stress into probability.
dispositionRationale: Official merchandise API rows, explicit no-return states, lagged Swiss input share and separate gross bank-nationality edges constitute a bounded comparison. Query nonreturn is not economic zero or universal source unavailability. Verizon primary OCF/cash/capex/debt comparator completes survivor investigation; WorldCom total-debt definition reconciled. Full identified causal matrix and private hedge detail are not acceptance requirements.

causalChain: A source-country rate/risk repricing can lead foreign investors or lenders to rebalance; portfolio, bank, FDI and trade-credit exposures can transmit through prices, rollover needs, FX demand and affiliate earnings. Currency depreciation can raise local-currency debt burdens for unhedged borrowers, while weaker collateral and cash flow can tighten credit. Local-currency funding, capital controls, reserves, hedges, domestic investors, trade substitution and policy support alter each regional link. The refreshed BIS CBS panel contains seven numeric 2026-Q1 gross international-claim observations reported by FR- and GB-nationality banking groups on DE, CH, US and FR residents; it returned no numeric rows for the selected US, CN or CH reporter series, or for selected CN counterpart-residence combinations. GB is not an EU reporter, and bank nationality is not country residence. The bounded 2024 UN Comtrade comparison provides four observed reporter-export flows (US↔China and EU27→US/China); Swiss-pair and US→EU requests returned no rows. A separate 2018 OECD input-output proxy records EU suppliers at 54% of Swiss imported intermediate inputs. These measures bound links only; none is a causal output multiplier.
counterEvidence: The latest BIS snapshot shows expanding cross-border bank credit, not generalized retreat. IMF April 2026 finds risk sensitivity varies by investor type and recipient vulnerabilities, and opportunities as well as risks accompany flows. US dollar, euro and CHF safe-asset/deep-market roles, China capital controls and largely domestic RMB funding, EU cross-border integration, and Switzerland’s external asset/liability structure mean the same shock does not transmit symmetrically. FDI is usually longer-horizon and less liquid than portfolio holdings, though it can still be delayed or revalued. Switzerland has diversified imports (OECD 2018 data: EU 54%, Asia 17%, North America 10%, rest of Europe 8%, other 11%); gross international claims do not net reciprocal positions, and observed cross-border bank credit expanded in Q1 2026. The available comparison is incomplete: UN Comtrade Switzerland-directed and US→EU queries returned count=0, not measured zero; no complete mirror or value-added series was assembled. EU-to-US and EU-to-China values are reported by EU27; the separate US-China mirror values differ substantially, as is expected for independently compiled export records.
stockFlowTransmission: BIS LBS and consolidated statistics are different exposure stocks (residence/intragroup versus nationality/ultimate-risk views); IMF IIP/CDIS/CPIS report positions. BOP records transactions/flows. Reconcile positions by opening stock + transactions + exchange/price valuation + other volume/reclassification changes = closing stock. OECD ICIO and BEA IO are annual production/trade flow structures, not financial exposures. Avoid summing positions and flows or double-counting cross-border intermediates and imported value added. Newly extracted BIS CBS claims are outstanding gross USD-equivalent stocks on an immediate-counterparty basis, while OECD Swiss input shares are 2018 production-input flow relationships. They cannot be added together or interpreted as net exposure; transactions, currency and valuation changes, maturity, hedges and domestic channels remain separate. Goods exports are annual nominal flows; BIS claims are quarterly gross consolidated stocks by bank nationality to counterparty residence; country IIP is a different residence-based position. They must not be summed or netted. FX valuation, service trade, firm ownership, maturities and hedging remain outside these measures.

CPIS/CDIS are incomplete and counterpart data may use immediate investor rather than ultimate risk. OECD ICIO 2025 ends in 2022 and the direct data archive was not extracted because the publisher endpoint returned an HTML CDN challenge; it is not treated as a complete 2026 flow matrix. causalChain: Historical episodes supply conditional sequences: credit-intensive investment and collateral expansion can precede deeper recessions; after losses, leverage, fixed obligations and limited refinancing can propagate the shock. A telecom infrastructure analogue can motivate testing oversupply, utilization, pricing, debt and salvage; the 2008–09 dollar funding crisis illustrates currency/maturity mismatch; property-price deflation episodes show collateral and private debt can interact. counterEvidence: Historical analogues are heterogeneous and selected ex post. BIS finds weak broad-sample association of goods/services price deflation with output, with stronger property/asset price relationships; even credit booms do not uniformly end in crisis. GAO’s Global Crossing record concerns a failed carrier and a specific contracting dispute, while contemporary large technology firms have broader cash-generative businesses, different debt and asset reuse options. Central banks and regulators now have different tools and frameworks than earlier episodes.
